B01:
Pick RAG when the answers change; fine-tune when the voice does. That one sentence settles most of the RAG-versus-fine-tuning argument, and the rest of the fight is about details that don't transfer between use cases.

RAG pulls from a live knowledge base at query time, so answers stay current and every claim can point back to a source document. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge and tone into the weights instead. No retrieval hop, so responses come back faster and sound consistent, but the model only knows what it knew on training day.

Here's the case that makes the trade-off concrete: a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. Retrieve from it? Fine-tune on it? Both? The honest answer depends on how often the content changes, whether your users need citations, and how much latency they'll tolerate. Those three questions do most of the deciding, so that's where we'll start.
B02:
A recent client had one core table carrying 23 indexes. We audited them, dropped 14, and write throughput doubled. Same hardware, same queries; the table just stopped doing unnecessary work on every write.

Indexes accumulate like that everywhere because the advice is always additive. Query slow? Add an index. Nobody comes back a year later to ask which ones still earn their keep.

But every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain every index on the table. An index that never serves a single query is still bloating your writes, inflating your storage, and stretching your vacuum cycles. Unused indexes are the most common indexing pitfall we see, and the most overlooked.

Below: the pitfalls that show up again and again in client audits, how to find the indexes nothing is reading in your own database, and a short checklist for keeping things lean.
B03:
Last year we onboarded 27 remote hires and cut our time-to-first-PR from 12 days to 5. New engineers now ship meaningful code in their first week instead of their third.

Every company claims to have remote onboarding figured out, right up until a new hire spends week one waiting for access, hunting for docs, and wondering who it's safe to ask. On a distributed team those small frictions don't just add up; they compound.

We got from 12 to 5 by making plenty of mistakes and running plenty of experiments. This guide is the playbook that survived: how we structure the first day, what onboarding buddies are actually for, which documentation earns its upkeep and which doesn't, and the metrics we track to keep improving.

The speed matters. But onboarding is also your first, best chance to show new hires how the team really works, which is why the details are worth sweating.
B04:
We surveyed 412 designers for The State of Design Systems 2026, across industries, company sizes, and levels of design maturity. The most telling number in the data: 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best.

That means a majority of teams are paying to build and maintain a system that isn't the source of truth it was pitched as. The component library exists. The products mostly route around it.

The reasons adoption stalls vary less than you'd expect. Unclear ownership. Competing priorities. Drift between design and code. Documentation nobody updates. The more useful finding sits on the other side: teams that get adoption right share habits consistent enough to copy, and this report spends most of its pages on those.

The rest of the report unpacks the numbers and the trends behind them, with takeaways you can bring back to your own team, wherever your system sits on the maturity curve.
B05:
It took me 14 months to build an emergency fund on a $52k salary. Nobody brags about a savings account at parties. There's no dopamine hit, no compounding chart to admire, and for long stretches the balance barely seemed to move.

The standard advice is 3-6 months of expenses, enough cushion to absorb a job loss, a medical bill, or a surprise car repair without reaching for a credit card. It sounds simple. For most people it's hard, and the hard part isn't the math. It's habits, trade-offs, and staying motivated while progress crawls.

So this is the post I wish I'd had at the start: the budget changes that mattered most, the automation that kept me consistent, and the mindset shifts that carried the slow middle stretch. If you've been putting off starting your emergency fund, or you started and stalled, it's written for you.

The average mid-market company uses 7 different tools just to buy things. Spreadsheets, email threads, ERP modules, standalone approval apps. Nobody chose that stack; it accumulated.

The cost shows up as a process nobody loves. Requests get lost between systems, approvers don't know what's waiting for them, and finance loses sight of committed spend. A simple purchase turns into a multi-week ordeal that frustrates everyone involved.

It doesn't have to work that way. Consolidating requests, approvals, and vendor management into a single workflow changes the numbers fast: companies that make the switch routinely see 14-day approval cycles drop to 3.

This post covers why procurement tooling got so fragmented in the first place, what a consolidated setup looks like day to day, and how to tell whether your organization is ready to make the change.

On Tuesday an expired TLS certificate on an internal service took us down for 4 hours. The service sat squarely in our request path, and when its certificate lapsed, the failures cascaded outward in ways that took real effort to trace. We know how disruptive the outage was, and this postmortem explains what happened and what we're changing.

The cause is humbling in its ordinariness. A certificate we didn't realize was close to expiry, on a service most of us rarely thought about, expired quietly and took a surprising amount of the stack down with it. Alerts fired, but the failure mode was confusing, and tracing the cascading errors back to their source took longer than it should have.

Below we walk through the full timeline and contributing factors, plus the 3 action items we're committing to: automated certificate-expiry monitoring across all services, documented rotation runbooks for every internal certificate, and regular game-day testing of certificate failure modes.

If you run internal TLS anywhere in your request path, it's worth checking today when your certificates expire. We wish we had.

The vertical SaaS playbook is being rewritten, and the tell is which markets suddenly look fundable.

The old objection was always market size. A niche industry might badly need better tools, but if the TAM couldn't support a venture-scale outcome, investors passed. AI changes that math. When a small team can build, sell, and support software that used to take fifty people, small vertical markets become viable. Attractive, even.

Marina software is our favorite example: a $400M TAM most funds would've ignored a decade ago. Today an AI-native team can serve that market profitably at a fraction of the historical cost structure, own the core workflow end to end, and expand over time into payments, insurance, and whatever else the workflow touches.

Our thesis is simple. The next generation of great vertical SaaS companies will be smaller teams attacking smaller markets and capturing far more of them. If you're building in this space, we'd love to hear from you.

T01:
I sent thousands of cold emails last year and finished at an 8% reply rate. Most cold email fails for boring, fixable reasons. The 5 things that actually moved my numbers:

1/ Four lines, max. Your prospect is scanning on their phone between meetings. Four lines is enough to say who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Anything longer gets archived.

2/ One CTA. Not two. Every additional ask cuts your response rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options every time.

3/ Personalize the first line, but only if it's real. "Loved your post on X" works when you actually read the post. One genuine sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most replies come from the 2nd or 3rd email, not the 1st. A polite bump is how deals happen. Silence is not a no.

5/ Track subject lines, send times, CTAs. I only hit 8% after treating cold email like a system instead of a lottery. Iterate weekly. That's the whole secret.
T02: Most meetings should be memos. Writing forces clarity, respects everyone's time, and leaves a record you can actually search. If an idea can't survive being written down, it won't survive a 60-minute meeting either.
T03:
19 months ago I launched a $49 one-time product. This week we crossed $10k MRR. No funding, no team, no audience. The playbook, in 4 tweets:

1/ Start ugly. V1 was a $49 one-time purchase: no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales, which was the whole point. It proved people would pay.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept coming back with the same recurring problem, and a one-time product couldn't serve it. Month 7, we moved to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks. Then it compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded every early customer personally, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote the roadmap for us.

4/ 19 months to $10k MRR isn't a rocket ship, and that's the point. Slow, compounding, profitable growth beats hype. If you're bootstrapping right now, keep going. It adds up.

T05:
New paper puts LLM-as-judge to the test: LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time, but only 64% on creative tasks. What that means if you use AI to evaluate AI:

1/ 81% overall agreement is strong. For routine evaluation tasks with clear criteria, an LLM judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ Creative tasks are where it breaks: when there's no objectively correct answer (style, originality, taste), agreement drops to 64%, and judges and humans part ways exactly where judgment matters most.

3/ One likely culprit: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length over real creativity. LLM judges like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ So use LLM judges for scale on objective tasks, and keep humans in the loop for creative work. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.

R01: Automated code review can reduce defect rates and reviewer workload, yet existing tools remain limited in scope and precision. We present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects directly within the pull-request workflow. We evaluate ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests drawn from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes. ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters, at a 12% false-positive rate that developers in our study characterized as acceptable for day-to-day use. The largest gains came in cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns, categories that traditional linters routinely miss. We also examine practical considerations for deploying automated review at scale, including reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines. Our findings suggest that automated code review can meaningfully augment, though not replace, human reviewers. We outline directions for future work, including adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning, and we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility.
R02:
To understand how enterprises are governing their data, we surveyed 156 organizations across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities.

The central finding: 44% of surveyed enterprises have no data-classification policy. Classification is the foundation the rest of governance depends on. Without it, incident response, access management, retention, and encryption rest on guesswork rather than policy, because no one can say consistently which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical.

The costs are concrete. Organizations without foundational governance report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and mounting friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close the gap, this whitepaper recommends a 5-step maturity model: data discovery, classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring. Each step includes concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria so teams can benchmark their progress.

Data governance now sits on the critical path for compliance, security, and AI readiness. The 44% figure suggests most enterprises have not yet organized around that fact.
R03:
At pilot firms using AI-assisted contract review, review time is down 60%. Work that once consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, and for legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less, that number is hard to ignore.

The caveat: hallucinated citations. AI tools can generate authorities that look entirely plausible and do not exist, and courts have shown little patience with filings that include them. Every AI-assisted output still needs qualified human review. No exceptions.

The professional guardrails are taking shape as well. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, centered on competence, confidentiality, and supervision. Adopt the technology; own the output.

For legal teams starting now, the path is unglamorous: begin with high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review, measure everything, and keep humans firmly in the loop. The firms that pair AI's speed with lawyers' judgment are the ones that will redefine what legal service looks like.
